newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Hebron unrest cools as south Lebanon heats up.
newsitem.headline: Hebron unrest cools as south Lebanon heats up.

text.p: The strife-torn West Bank town of Hebron was mainly quiet on Sunday after a week of Arab-Israeli clashes but Palestinians seethed over torn copies of the Koran in a ransacked school.

"Today the situation is calming," Palestinian West Bank Preventive Security chief Jibril Rajoub told Reuters. "Our people expressed themselves in a series of demonstrations last week. They did their national duty."

In south Lebanon, the simmering conflict between the Jewish state and Iranian-backed Hizbollah (Party of God) guerrillas heated into artillery duels and Israeli air strikes after Hizbollah forces killed an Israeli officer.
In Jerusalem, a political crisis between Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Foreign Minister David Levy showed no signs of cooling.
Hebron has been the scene of daily street unrest since an Israeli woman put up posters on Arab shops depicting the Prophet Mohammad as a pig stamping on the Koran nine days ago.

On Sunday, Palestinians found torn copies of the Koran among a pile of books in a sacked schoolroom near the confrontation line between Israeli- and PLO-run sectors of the city and said Israeli soldiers were responsible.

"The army always breaks the door and comes in to use the roof to watch demonstrators. They broke furniture and we found four Koran books torn and thrown on the ground," said the elementary school's headmaster, Arifeh Ebedo.
"Where are the Moslems all over the world who see their holy books torn, thrown and trampled?" she said."
An Israeli officer said after touring the school with his Palestinian counterpart that Israeli soldiers were not involved.
"Colonel Nagar made clear and emphasised...that Israeli soldiers had no part in this incident," said Peter Lerner, spokesman for the Israeli military's Civil Administration.
"The investigation showed that the room was locked and that soldiers did not have access to it...there were no forced entry signs on the door," Lerner said.
In the last active Arab-Israeli front in south Lebanon, Israeli army officer Major Nadav Milo, 24, was killed in a clash between soldiers and Hizbollah guerrillas.
Hizbollah guerrillas are fighting to oust Israeli troops and their local militia allies from the 15-km (nine-mile)-wide border zone they hold in south Lebanon.

In retaliation, Israeli planes launched three separate raids on Hizbollah positions in the area. Israeli artillery also engaged the guerrillas in duels in which three Lebanese civilians, including two boys, were wounded.
Israeli security sources said six or seven rounds of mortar fire landed on the border between Israel and south Lebanon.
Milo was the 12th Israeli soldier to be killed in Lebanon this year. Last year, 27 Israeli soldiers died in Lebanon.
In Jerusalem, Netanyahu failed to defuse a lingering political crisis over Foreign Minister Levy's threat to resign.
Levy fears his status as formal coordinator of peace talks policy could be eroded by the expected ascent of hawkish ex-general Ariel Sharon to the vacant post of finance minister.
A Sunday meeting between the two men ended with no results, casting doubt on whether Netanyahu would be able to present a long-awaited cabinet shake-up to parliament on Monday.
Levy has promised an answer soon on whether he will resign. If he were to bolt, Netanyahu would be left with the barest of parliamentary majorities, possibly forcing new elections.
In the Gaza Strip, the Israeli army on Sunday blew up two tunnels it said were dug illicitly by Palestinians for smuggling weapons from Egypt to PLO-ruled Gaza.
